fields.h1: What Is the Love of God?
fields.meta_title: What Is the Love of God? Understanding God’s Love
fields.description: God is love — strong, faithful, unconditional, and proved at the cross. Here is what Scripture reveals about the love of God, and why nothing can separate us from it.
fields.body_html:
The Bible makes one of the most staggering claims ever written about God: not merely that God loves, but that “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Love is not one of God’s moods or one item on a list of his attributes; it is the very heart of who he is. Everything he does flows from it. And this love is not the sentimental, fickle thing our culture often means by the word. It is strong, faithful, holy, and free — a love that gives everything, endures everything, and will never let its own go. To grasp even a little of the love of God is to have the foundation of a settled, joyful life.

So what is the love of God actually like? Scripture describes it not in abstractions but in action, supremely at the cross. Here are its great features — enough to steady the anxious and melt the hard.

God’s love gives — it is proved at the cross

The Bible never lets us define God’s love by our feelings or our circumstances; it points us always to a historical act. “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10). Love, in the divine dictionary, is self-giving. It is measured not by words but by what it will surrender for the beloved — and God surrendered his Son.

This is why the cross is the anchor of Christian assurance. When we cannot feel God’s love, we can look at Calvary and know it: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Jesus himself named this the highest love there is: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13) — and then he laid down his life for those who were not yet his friends but his enemies. The love of God is not a feeling he has about us; it is a price he paid for us.

God’s love is unconditional — he loved us first

Human love is usually a response: we love what is lovely, what pleases us, what loves us back. God’s love runs the other way. It does not wait to be earned or deserved; it takes the initiative toward the undeserving. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Before we ever turned to him, before we had done anything to attract his favour, his love was already set upon us.

This is what makes God’s love so secure. Because it did not begin with our goodness, it does not end with our failure. God declares to his people, “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you” (Jeremiah 31:3). An everlasting love has no starting point in our merit and no ending point in our sin. It is not a reward for the deserving but a gift to the ruined — and that is precisely why it holds.

God’s love is faithful and never fails

The love of God is not a flame that flickers but a covenant that holds. In the ruins of Jerusalem, when everything else had collapsed, Jeremiah found his footing here: “The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23). God’s love is not exhausted by our sin nor worn out by our slowness; every morning it is fresh again.

The Psalmist heaps up images to convey how vast and tender it is: “as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him... As a father shows compassion to his children, so the Lord shows compassion to those who fear him” (Psalm 103:11, 13). It is both immense and intimate — as boundless as the sky and as personal as a father bending over a hurting child. This is the love that will not let us go.

God’s love delights in us

Many believe God tolerates them, or puts up with them for Christ’s sake, but cannot imagine that he actually delights in them. Scripture says otherwise, in language almost too warm to believe. God “will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing” (Zephaniah 3:17). The God of the universe sings over his people with joy. He is not a grudging benefactor but a rejoicing Father.

John invites us simply to stand and marvel at it: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). We are not merely forgiven criminals kept at arm’s length; we are adopted children, brought into the family, loved with the same love the Father has for his Son. To be a Christian is to be caught up in a love older than the world and to be told, astonishingly, that God is glad to have us.

God’s love is holy, not indulgent

Because God’s love is so tender, we can mistake it for mere indulgence — as though a loving God must simply approve of whatever we do. But real love wills the good of the beloved, and God loves us too much to leave us as we are. His love is holy, and it therefore refuses to be content with our ruin. This is why he disciplines his children: “The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). Far from disproving his love, God’s correction proves it; an indifferent father lets his child run into the road, but a loving one intervenes.

So when God’s dealings with us are hard, we must not conclude that he has stopped loving us. Often his love is most at work precisely in the painful pruning that makes us fruitful. The risen Christ said even to a church he rebuked, “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19). God’s love is not a soft sentiment that overlooks our sin; it is a strong, purifying fire that is determined to make us like his Son. That is a far greater love than mere approval could ever be — it loves us enough to change us.

Nothing can separate us from God’s love

The final glory of God’s love is its unbreakable security. Paul climbs to the summit of his letter to the Romans and plants his flag there: “I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). He lists every threat he can think of and dismisses them all. Nothing in the universe can pry the believer from the grip of God’s love.

This is the ground on which a fearful soul can finally rest. Your standing before God does not rise and fall with your performance, because it never rested on your performance in the first place. It rests on his love, and his love is stronger than death. Paul’s deepest prayer for the church was that they might “know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:19) — a love so vast that we will spend eternity exploring it and never reach its edge.

How to live in the love of God

How do we come to know this love, not just as a doctrine but as an experience? First, we receive it — for it is a gift, given freely in Christ to all who will trust him. We do not work up to God’s love; we rest in it. And then we abide in it. Jesus said, “Abide in my love” (John 15:9) — make your home there, return to it daily, let it be the settled climate of your soul.

The believers through the centuries who have loved God most were not those who first loved him best, but those who most deeply grasped how much they were loved. Love received becomes love returned; a heart warmed by the love of God cannot help loving him back, and loving others with the love it has received. This is the whole engine of the Christian life — not striving to earn a love we already have, but living out of a love that has already found us. So make it your daily study. Look often at the cross. Rehearse the promises. When your feelings say you are unloved, preach the cross to yourself until your feelings fall into line behind the fact. And let this be the rock beneath your feet in every storm: you are loved by God with an everlasting, unbreakable, delighting love — a love that chose you before the world began and will hold you when the world is gone — and nothing will ever change it.
